title: Water by Hand: A Human-Powered UV Device and Questions for a Field Trial
subtitle: The TEHG-UV runs on a crank or pedal. Its laboratory results are promising; finding a use for it starts with the water people collect and the effort treatment would require.
excerpt: A crank or pedal powers a UV lamp. The next questions concern water quality, everyday use and repairs: what would it take to try the device outside the laboratory?

content.text: Four liters a day had to cover drinking, washing and cooking for each resident of Dabat Bosin, Sudan, in 2024, according to UNHCR. That is 20 percent of its 20-liter daily minimum for post-emergency conditions.
Published in ACS Nano in February 2026, this paper describes a manual prototype, TEHG-UV, utilizing ultraviolet light to inactivate microorganisms in water a household already has.

Combining manual power (pedaling or hand cranking), a triboelectric nanogenerator (TENG), and electromagnetic generator (EMG) provides sufficient power to operate a UV mercury lamp. The researchers tested batch disinfection without grid electricity.
Addressing Household Water Challenges

As documented in UNHCR’s 2024 WASH report, emergency installations in Chad provided nearly 13 liters per person per day after more than 239 thousand Sudanese refugees arrived. Where water from the installed facilities is contaminated, the technology may help. In addition, shortages necessitate further remedies for water collection, distribution, and infrastructure improvements.

A household may practice boiling, chlorinating water, using portable UV light, or combining methods. Individuals must evaluate each solution based on energy requirements, proper dosages, contact time, and others. Chlorination can leave disinfectants for residual protection of stored water. UV disinfection requires sufficiently clear water prior to treatment and appropriate storage after treatment.
One lamp, two electrical demands
Starting a mercury lamp and keeping it on require different electrical outputs. That’s why the researchers combined a triboelectric nanogenerator (TENG) with an electromagnetic generator (EMG).

Contact between polyurethane and PTFE surfaces generates charges within TENG. Meanwhile, mechanical rotations alter magnetic flux through coils in the EMG, generating electricity. While TENG produces higher voltage output, EMG delivers greater current output after ignition. A transmission connects both generators to the user's motion.
Existing UV disinfection equipment is available in battery-powered forms.
Experimental Results

Laboratory tests demonstrate a 25-minute hand-cranked disinfection achieving eight log reductions in the test microorganisms for 2-liter batches and a 15-minute pedaled disinfection reaching eight log reductions for ten-liter batches. Eight log reductions imply a reduction by a factor of one hundred million (99.999999%) under the reported test conditions. Safety assessments should factor in quality of source water and post-disinfection water management practices.

Supplementary tests using 500 mL batches, with five replicates, demonstrated an eight-log reduction within five minutes of mechanical action (80 RPM) in each of three organisms (E.coli, B.subtilis, and MS2 Bacteriophage).

Source water samples were taken from the Tsinghua River in Beijing. For the November samples, the extra tables list the turbidity levels ranging from 2.6 NTU to 2.8 NTU. Much cloudier water needs further testing because particles can interfere with UV treatment.

WHO guidelines define the highest household drinking-water treatment performance category as requiring at least 4-log reduction of bacteria, 5 logs of viruses, and 4 logs of protozoa. Assessment requires evidence for these organism groups under the relevant test conditions. Eight-log results alone do not establish a WHO classification for this invention.
Cost Assessments

The researchers put the annual cost at about $8.57 per person, using a levelized-cost model that includes parts, production and expected replacement intervals. The estimate is not a purchase price or a measured cost from a humanitarian project.

A pilot budget would incorporate local manufacturing or purchase costs, transportation expenses, replacement costs, training for users, water sample testing, expected component life-span revisions based on evidence from use, among others.
Needs for Field Tests

Analyzing the water condition at proposed sites would come first. This approach does not remove dissolved chemical contaminants and heavy metals from water. Pre-filtration may improve UV disinfection effectiveness by reducing particle content. However, eliminating chemical contaminants needs removal treatments suited to the substances present. Common sand filtration cannot be assumed to address the issue.

Can users consistently keep cranking or pedaling for the full treatment time? The trial would need to include people with limited strength or mobility. It should check what happens if someone stops early, how users spot a fault, and whether spare lamps and repairs are available.

UV treatment does not leave a protective disinfectant residual in water. After treatment, storage and dispensing require adequate precautions against recontamination. The design also needs protection against harmful UV exposure and mercury lamp breakage, plus a way to collect and dispose of used lamps.

A 2025 review by Jeon et al. in Micromachines examines triboelectric power generation for disinfection. Kim et al. studied a walking-powered water-bottle system in Nature Water in 2024, while Huo et al. discussed contact electrification for personal sanitation in a 2025 commentary. None of these papers reports field-test results for TEHG-UV.
